title: "Be," and it is
hookLine: His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say be, and it is (36:82)

lines: A MAN CRUSHES AN OLD BONE.
cards: A man walks up holding an old bone, dry and crumbling, picked up from some forgotten grave. He crushes it in his fist, and the dust falls between his fingers.
Then he asks the question that's been his whole argument: who could bring this back to life? Anyone who's stood at a funeral has asked a version of it.
Surah Ya-Sin ends by answering him, and the answer comes down to a single word of two letters in Arabic.

teach.b: Verse seventy-eight. He coins a comparison for Us, Allah says, and forgets his own creation. He asks, who will revive bones once they've rotted away?

teach.h: THE ONE WHO MADE THEM FIRST.
teach.b: Verse seventy-nine answers: the One who brought them into being the first time will revive them. He knows every creation. The man forgot that he himself was once nothing.
If starting a person from nothing was possible, starting again from dust is no harder.
Verse eighty adds a picture: the One who makes fire for you from the green tree. Something living and wet, and out of it comes flame. Then the line the whole surah has been walking toward.
Pickthall: "But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is."

teach.h: KUN, FA-YAKUN: BE, AND IT IS.
teach.b: In Arabic: kun, fa-yakun. Kun is two letters, kaf and nun. Muslims understand this as the Qur'an's way of describing Allah's power, not a picture of Allah speaking like a person: no effort, no delay, no materials needed.
The Qur'an uses the phrase in several places: for the creation of the heavens and earth, for the birth of 'Isa, Jesus, and here, for raising the dead.
Then the last verse of Ya-Sin: glory to Him in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you'll be brought back. This is why the surah is read beside the dying.
The question in that room is the man's question: can this come back? Ya-Sin's answer is the first answer again: the One who began it from nothing can begin it again.

how: Muslims often say 'kun fa-yakun' when speaking of Allah's power to bring about what seems impossible, and the closing verses of Ya-Sin are commonly recited at funerals and by the dying.

o: kun: Allah's command, and the thing simply is
the first breath given to Adam's body of clay
the fire brought out of the green tree

games.q: the end of Ya-Sin — tap the pairs.
p: the One who made them first

s: kun fa-yakun appears only once in the Qur'an
it appears in several places, including for the heavens and earth and the birth of 'Isa.
Ya-Sin answers the bone question by pointing to the first creation
the One who brought them into being the first time will revive them.
kun is a long word in Arabic
it's two letters, kaf and nun.

games.q: a man crushes a dry bone and asks: who could bring this back to life? what does Ya-Sin answer first?
o: the One who made it the first time.
games.why: the One who brought them into being the first time. the man had forgotten his own creation.

practice: In the verse, there's no gap between the command and the thing; a life is full of gaps. Think of one task you've been putting off, a call, a form, an apology, and picture only its very first step, small enough for a minute.
If you pray, you can say bismillah over it, and sit quietly with the decision made.

wordCard.voice: Be. Kun, the word of Allah's command in Ya-Sin's closing verses: He says to a thing be, and it is, and so He can raise the dead. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: be, and it is. kun is just two letters, kaf and nun.

carryVoice: Your line: no harder the second time. Two letters, kaf and nun. That's day five hundred fifty-one.
